original_value: Learning how to program is becoming essential in many disciplines. However, programming cannot be easily learned, especially by non-engineering students. It is challenging to conduct engineering education for non-engineering majored students. Therefore, it is important to teach non-engineering students to learn with efficient learning strategies. To discover an efficient learning strategy, we had 64 students practice programming with a simple learning management system and tracked all of their practice behaviors on multiple choice questions. The learning management system assigned one multiple choice question per day, but let students themselves decide their own practice frequencies. Students could also make unsynchronized communications by commenting on the questions. By analyzing their behavior patterns and other performance indicators, this paper compared the effect of two different practice strategies for multiple choice questions: distributed practice and massed practice. Our analysis found that students who adopted distributed practice significantly outperformed those who adopted massed practice on final exams (p=0.031). We further explored the possible reasons that led to this significant difference. Students who adopted distributed practice strategy tended to make higher percentage of first submission correctness, be more cautious while correcting errors, and be more constructive in posting question-related comments.

result.paraphrase: Learning to program is increasingly essential across many fields, yet it is not easy to master, particularly for students outside engineering. Teaching engineering concepts to non-engineering majors is challenging, so helping these students learn with effective strategies is important. To identify an efficient approach, we had 64 students practice programming using a simple learning management system and recorded all of their practice behaviors on multiple-choice questions. The system provided one multiple-choice question per day, while students chose how often to practice on their own. They could also communicate asynchronously by commenting on the questions. By examining behavior patterns and other performance indicators, this paper compared two practice methods for multiple-choice questions: distributed practice and massed practice. Our analysis showed that students using distributed practice significantly outperformed those using massed practice on final exams (p=0.031). We also investigated possible reasons for this difference. Students who used distributed practice tended to achieve a higher rate of correct first submissions, act more cautiously when fixing mistakes, and write more constructive question-related comments.
